title: Probability distributions
keyIdea: A random variable X gives a number to each outcome of an experiment, such as the total of two dice. Its probability distribution lists every value x with its probability P(X = x), in a table or a bar graph. Every probability is between 0 and 1, and together they sum to 1. You can build a distribution from theory, by counting equally likely outcomes, or estimate one from data using relative frequencies.

kid: Roll two dice and add the scores. The total is a random variable, written with a capital letter: X. A small letter, x, stands for one value it can take. X can be any whole number from 2 to 12.

There are 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes. Count the ones that give each total. Seven comes from six pairs: (1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 3), (5, 2) and (6, 1). So P(X = 7) = 6/36. A total of 12 comes only from (6, 6), so P(X = 12) = 1/36. The totals are not equally likely.

A table of every value and its probability is the probability distribution. Two rules always hold. Each probability is between 0 and 1, and all of them add to 1. Use the sum to find an unknown. If P(X = x) = kx for x = 1, 2, 3 and 4, then k + 2k + 3k + 4k = 10k = 1, so k = 0.1.

Read the signs with care. P(X ≤ 4) includes 4, so it is 1/36 + 2/36 + 3/36 = 6/36. P(X < 4) leaves 4 out, so it is 3/36. You can also estimate a distribution from data. Roll the dice many times and divide each count by the number of rolls. These relative frequencies get close to the model, but they are rarely exact.
adult: This topic is part of the A level Mathematics content on discrete probability distributions. Students should understand and use simple discrete distributions, with the binomial as a key example. In the US Common Core, standards S-MD.1, 3 and 4 ask students to define a random variable, graph its distribution, and find probabilities from theory or from data.

Key terms: sample space, outcome, discrete random variable, probability distribution (or probability function), P(X = x), cumulative probability P(X ≤ x) and relative frequency. A distribution is valid when no P(X = x) is below 0 and the probabilities sum to 1. A new variable from the same outcomes has a new distribution. For Y, the larger of two dice, P(Y = y) = (2y − 1)/36.

Common mistakes: assuming the values of X are equally likely, so P(X = 7) is taken as 1/11. Setting k = 1/n when P(X = x) = kx. Treating P(X < 4) as P(X ≤ 4). Accepting a negative probability because the list sums to 1. Calling a relative frequency the exact probability. Take care with notation as well: capital X is the variable and small x is one of its values.

In the lab the learner taps the 36 cells of a two-dice grid to build the distribution of the total. They slide k until kx sums to 1, and drag a cut to shade P(X ≤ 4), P(X < 4) and P(X ≥ 10). They roll 10, 100 and 1000 times and watch the relative frequencies settle near the model. Last, they build the distribution of the larger score from the same grid.

familyTip: Roll two dice 50 times together and tally the totals. Before you start, each person bets on the most common total; then compare the tally with the 6/36 for seven.

visual.caption: Could this list be a probability distribution? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: build the two-dice total from 36 outcomes, slide k until kx sums to 1, shade ≤ and <, roll 1000 times, then build the larger score.

practice.prompt: X is the total of two fair dice. Which value of X is most likely?
practice.hint: Count the pairs of scores that give each total out of the 36 outcomes.
practice.explain: Seven comes from 6 of the 36 outcomes, more than any other total, so P(X = 7) = 6/36 is the largest.

practice.prompt: X is the total of two fair dice. How many of the 36 equally likely outcomes give X = {t}?
practice.hint: List the pairs (first die, second die) that add to {t}, starting with (1, {=t-1}).
practice.explain: The pairs are (1, {=t-1}) up to ({=t-1}, 1), which is {=t-1} outcomes, so P(X = {t}) = {=t-1}/36.

practice.prompt: P(X = x) = kx for x = 1, 2, 3, 4. What is k?
practice.hint: The probabilities must sum to 1. Write the sum in terms of k.
practice.explain: k + 2k + 3k + 4k = 10k = 1, so k = 0.1. The value 0.25 would only work if every probability were equal.

practice.prompt: A discrete random variable takes the values 1, 2 and 3. P(X = 1) = 0.{a} and P(X = 2) = 0.{b}. Find P(X = 3).
practice.hint: All the probabilities in a distribution add up to 1.

pool.prompt: Which list could be the probabilities of a probability distribution?
pool.hint: Check both rules: no probability below 0 or above 1, and a sum of exactly 1.
pool.explain: 0.3 + 0.3 + 0.4 = 1 with no negatives. The second sums to 1.5, and the third has a negative probability.

pool.prompt: X is the total of two fair dice. How many of the 36 outcomes give X ≤ {c}?
pool.hint: Add the outcomes for each total: a total of 2 has 1, a total of 3 has 2, and so on, up to {c}.

pool.prompt: X is the total of two fair dice. What is P(X < 4)?
pool.hint: “<” is strict, so 4 is not included. Which totals are less than 4?
pool.explain: Only totals 2 and 3: 1/36 + 2/36 = 3/36. The answer 6/36 is P(X ≤ 4).

pool.prompt: Y is the larger score when two fair dice are rolled. What is P(Y = 6)?
pool.hint: Count the cells in the 6 × 6 grid where at least one die shows 6.
pool.explain: Six cells have a 6 on the first die and six have a 6 on the second. (6, 6) is in both, so there are 6 + 6 − 1 = 11 outcomes and P(Y = 6) = 11/36.

pool.prompt: A fair die is rolled {=6*n} times. How many sixes would you expect?
pool.hint: P(6) = 1/6. Multiply by the number of rolls.
pool.explain: {=6*n} × 1/6 = {n} sixes. The real count will vary around this.

pool.prompt: A spinner landed on red 43 times in 100 spins. Which statement is best?
pool.hint: Is a result from data the true probability, or an estimate of it?
pool.explain: 43/100 = 0.43 is a relative frequency. It estimates P(red); more spins give a better estimate.

pool.prompt: P(X = x) = kx for x = 1, 2, 3, 4. Find P(X = {x}).
pool.hint: First find k from the rule that the probabilities sum to 1.

pool.prompt: In the notation P(X = x), what does the capital X stand for?
pool.hint: One letter names the variable and the other names a value. Which is which?
pool.explain: Capital X is the random variable; small x is a particular value, such as 7.
